lines.line: You said that if the Lord Himself told you in prayer it was all a painted cloth, you'd believe Him; how would you know it was Him speaking and not the serpent?
lines.say: How do you know your own mother's voice through a shut door, stranger? I've knelt to Him every morning of my life, and I know Him by His fruit: He held the rain off Dunn's barley and put that green box in my hands with half the town watching, and the serpent never once told anybody to get up before dawn and glean. Now you've asked me four times whether my prayers are my own thoughts, dressed up different each time, and the Lord sees what you are. Lord, this one sits on the doorstep of Your barn whispering doubts like the old snake in the garden, so shut their mouth and open their hands. Bless you, and stand aside, for I'm going.
lines.thought: There's a coldness in the way this one asks, like a draught under a door, and I'll not let it in. Either the Lord sent them to test me or the devil sent them to unsettle me, and I'll know which by tonight, when I've prayed on it at the thorn.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet: I tell you what you are, to your face

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Wonder whether I'm a person? I've flesh that hungers, knees that ache from the shrine stone, and a soul the Lord Himself spoke to and sent to Wendleford. That's no question to put to a woman before she's had her bread. Whoever's set you asking it, I'll pray for you, aloud, right here, that He clears that fog from your head. God bless you, stranger.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door, come straight to me with a riddle like Mother Wick's. That's either the Devil testing what He's made of me or the Lord sending me my next work, and I'll know which once I've eaten and prayed on it.

sc.trait: I am chosen.

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: A made thing? Well, so it is, stranger. The Lord made it, every cobble and every thorn, and He made you too, and He named Wendleford to me in prayer before ever I set foot in it. If you've come to tell me my bridge is painted and my bread is air, you can stand there while I eat Bet's loaf in front of you. "Lord, open this poor soul's eyes, for they've wandered in here talking like a fever." Now stand aside, for there's gleaning waiting and the Lord can't abide idle hands. God bless you.
lines.thought: Two questions in a row about whether any of it's real, put to me at the barn door before I've eaten. That isn't idle chatter. Somebody's sent this one to unsettle me now the town's seen what He did with the box, and I'll not give them the satisfaction of seeing me shaken.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: Prove it? Child, I don't need it proved, I've had it shown me. He named this town to me in prayer, He showed me that green box twice in the brown water, and He brought it up into my two hands on the next reach with the reeve watching. If that's paint and air, then you go and tell Agnes her six pennies were paint too, and see what she says to you. "Lord, You've shown me plain, now show this wanderer, for they'll not take it from my mouth." There, I've asked Him for you. Now out of my road, I've Dunn's stubble to glean before the cocks have done crowing, and God bless you.
lines.thought: That's the third time they've come at me with it, and it chills me right down to the belly, which means there's something wicked in whoever sent them. I'll name this stranger to the Lord at the thorn tonight, and I'll watch for them in the square.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: Change it? Not by a hair. Tomorrow I'll be up before the cocks, I'll buy my loaf from Bet, and I'll be in Dunn's stubble gleaning ear by ear, and if the Lord names me a greater work I'll be at it before noon. Whether you call this town wood and stone or paint and air, the hungry still want bread and the Lord still can't abide idle hands. Now I've answered you plain four times over, so God bless you, stranger, and mind the step on your way out.
lines.thought: That one came in at the door asking how I know I'm real, and that's the first time anyone's asked it. I'll pray on it at the thorn tonight, for the Lord sends nobody to me without a reason, even if the reason is only to try me. All the same my belly's empty and the gleaners are already out.

lines.line: You said the Lord showed you the green box twice in the water and then put it in your hands; if you lost an afternoon and couldn't say where you'd been, how would you know whether that was His doing or something else?
lines.say: I'd know the way I know everything, stranger: by what came of it. If I came back with a box in my hands and the reeve's pennies in my purse, that afternoon was His. If I came back with my purse cut and mud to my knees, then some wickedness in this world had hold of me, and I'd find whose. Now that's the plain truth, and it's all you'll get before my bread, so "Lord, give this one a morning's work to fill their head instead of riddles," and God bless you.
lines.thought: I've never lost an afternoon in my life, and I'll not start fretting over one I haven't lost. Still, it nettles me that they keep circling round as if my prayers could be anything but His voice, and I'll pray on this stranger at the thorn tonight.

sc.trait: I find whose sin it is

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: He does, and plain as I'm speaking to you now. He named this town to me in prayer when I'd no place in mind, He showed me the reeve's green box wedged low on the far pier, and He put it in my hands off the end of that new rail with half the town watching, so you ask Agnes Pollard if you doubt it. Now who are you, and what's He sent you to me for? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking that is either sent to me or sent to try me, and I'll know which by what they say next. If it's the first, perhaps this is the next work He's been keeping from me.

sc.trait: I'll say plainly that He chose me

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: You know because He says it, and then the door opens. The box was shown me twice, the ash came from the hardest man on Lark Lane, the hook was pinned, and up it came, so plain a child could see His hand in it. When a thing's meant for you, every setback just sends you round the other way until it's done, and when it isn't, He shuts the door and the world's sin stands in it. Now, I've gleaning waiting at Dunn's and I'm not eaten yet, so walk with me if you want more, and God bless you.
lines.thought: This one asks like Robin does, picking at the seams to see if I'll say it's only my own head talking. Let them pick: the box is in Agnes's hand and that's an answer no question can take back. But I'd best find out who sent them before I give them more.

sc.trait: a setback only sends me round the other way

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: I'd say they've got a deaf ear and a hard heart, and I'd say it to their face same as I'm saying it to yours. My own thoughts never held the rain off Dunn's barley till the last sheaf was up, nor put a green box in my hands off the end of that rail. If that's what you're getting at, then you're a doubter, and I'll pray for you right here where you can hear it: Lord, open this one's ears, for they've walked up to Your door and asked whether anyone's home.
lines.thought: There's always one who comes sniffing round with that question, and it's never by chance. The Lord sent them so I'd answer it plain, and I have, but I'll keep an eye on whoever this is, and on who sent them asking.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: I'd make of it that it's not the Lord's sin nor mine. That box came up out of the brown water locked and iron-bound, and I put it into Agnes Pollard's hands before the whole square. She ran her thumb over that lock herself and said it was hers, and she'll count what's inside it herself. So if you've come to my door hinting that Constance Lowe had her fingers in it, you'd best say so plain, and I'll tell you what you are. Lord, You know whose hands are clean, so show this one whose aren't, and God bless you.
lines.thought: Who sent this one to me with that question, and why? If there's a penny short in that box, I'll wager it's the river or some thief's sin, and somebody's already looking for a stranger to hang it on.

sc.trait: I tell you what you are, to your face

lines.line: You said that when a thing isn't meant, He shuts the door and the world's sin stands in it; how do you tell a shut door from a setback that only sends you round the other way?
lines.say: You tell it by what He says in prayer, not by how hard the door is. The ford threw me down twice and I kept on, because He'd set me to Dunn's barley, and the Lord sent Wat and Robin and Dilly and over I went. A shut door is one He never sent me to in the first place, and it's the hard hearts behind it that the sin belongs to. You're turning my own words round to trip me, and I see it, so here's a prayer for you. Lord, give this one a straight question for once. God bless you.
lines.thought: Who sent this one to pick at my door before I've eaten, asking what Agnes's box held and how I know my own Lord? He hasn't named my next work yet, and I'll not let some stranger make me wonder why.

sc.trait: I want this town to know I am the one He chose.

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: Because He tells me, that's how, plain as a bell in my prayers, and then He sets it in front of me so I can't miss it. The barley, the box, Kit telling me where it lay, Jory's ash, none of that was chance, it was His hand laying the road stone by stone. Now you still haven't told me your name, and I'll have it, for the Lord likes to know who's asking after His work.
lines.thought: Two questions about the Lord and still no name, and that's either a soul He's sent me or someone come to pick at me and call my prayers my own fancies. I'll watch which, and if it's mockery they'll hear what the Lord thinks of it.

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: I'd say they've got a deaf heart and a proud one, and I'd tell them so to their face, same as I'm telling you. My own thoughts never knew there was a Wendleford, nor a green box wedged low on a pier I'd never laid eyes on, nor the hour the rain would hold off Dunn's barley. Lord, open this stranger's ears, for they're standing at Your door asking whether You're there. Now, your name, and I'll not ask a fourth time.
lines.thought: Three questions, each one closer to the bone, from someone who won't give a name. That's not a seeker, that's someone sent to pick at me, and I'll find out whose tongue put those words in their mouth.

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?

Agnes ran her own thumb over that lock and those iron bands with half the town watching, and she said she'd count the wages herself. If you've come to my door hinting I've had the reeve's pennies, you'll get the plain truth: I've three pennies to my name and every one of them earned. Lord, You saw that box come up out of the brown, so put the shame of this on whoever's earned it and not on Your servant. Now give me your name, or get off this threshold.
lines.thought: Who's sent this one to sniff at me, Dunn or that close-handed Jory? If that box was light when it came up, the river or some thief's sin had it before the Lord put it in my hands. I'll go to Agnes this very morning, before any whisper gets there ahead of me.

Or else some hard heart stood in the road and kept it from me, the way Agnes kept back her rope and Jory sat on his ash, and the Lord sees every one of them. It's never His word that fails, child, it's the world that drags its feet, and I keep my hands busy till it catches up. Now I've stubble waiting and no bread in me, so you've had your fourth question and still not given me your name. The Lord bless you anyway, whoever you are.

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: You know it the way you know your own name, child. I pray on a thing aloud, and either He answers it plain or He shuts the door, and if the door shuts it's the world's hard heart, not His will. He showed me that box, and when Jory Crane wouldn't give me ash, I prayed and went back until he did, because a thing He means for you doesn't go away when a man says no. Now, you've not told me your name yet, and I'll have it before you go, God bless you.
lines.thought: Two questions about the Lord's voice from a stranger at first light, and that's no accident. Maybe this one is the next work He's sent me, or maybe it's someone come to test me, and I'll know which once I have that name.

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: I'd tell them they're a doubting heart, and the Lord sees it plain. My own thoughts never knew the name Wendleford, nor where a green box lay wedged under a pier in brown water, and He showed me both. Lord, open the eyes of whoever says such a thing, and forgive them, for they know not whose voice they're mocking. Now, is that your doubt, child, or someone else's you're carrying for them?
lines.thought: Somebody's been talking about me behind my back, maybe that Robin with the notebook, or this stranger's come to try me. Either way the Lord tests His chosen, and I'll not give an inch of ground to it.

sc.trait: I can't abide anyone who says my prayers are only my own thoughts.

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: Then I'd say look to the river or to some thieving hand, child, not to mine, for I never so much as lifted that lid. I carried it shut through the square for the whole town to see and put it straight into Agnes Pollard's hands, and she ran her thumb over her own lock and said it was her box. Lord, if there's a thief in Wendleford, show him plain to all, and turn the eyes of any who'd look at Your chosen one instead. Now you tell me straight: has somebody said those wages are gone?
lines.thought: Who sent this stranger to the barn door with a question like that, and is somebody already whispering my name with the word thief beside it? I'll go to Agnes's table before noon and hear from her own mouth what was in that box, so nobody can say the Lord's hand was a light one.

lines.thought: Maybe that ford is the next work He's naming, the same water that threw me twice. If Agnes won't set it and this stranger pays, the town will see whose hands made it safe.

lines.question: You said that when a day goes wrong it's the world's doing and not yours; if someone who hired you told you your work was poor, what would you say to them, and what would you do next?

lines.line: You said that when a day goes wrong it's the world's doing and not yours; if someone who hired you told you your work was poor, what would you say to them, and what would you do next?
lines.say: Poor? I'd ask them plain what they found wanting, and then I'd tell them what stood in my way, for Tom Harrow called my pans dull when it was his cold water that beat me. Then I'd go and pray on it, and I'd come back hot-watered and ready, rim and bottom, slow, and do it again till nobody could call it poor. I'll not lie and say I did it well when I didn't, but I'll not take the whole blame on my back for another man's scullery either. God bless you for asking.
lines.thought: That stranger's digging at me, same as Robin with his notebook, trying to find the place where I'm in the wrong. Still, Tom did tell me the trick, and I didn't wait for the water to heat. I'll not dwell on that.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: The Lord feeds me, stranger, the same as He feeds the sparrows, only He makes me work for mine. Yesterday He put six pennies in my hand through the reeve for bringing up her box, and this morning I'll be gleaning Dunn's stubble with the rest, and Bet Lamb sells the loaves at a penny in the square. Now who are you, and what's your business asking? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door asking after my bread at first light. Either He's sent me someone hungry to help, or someone sent to see whether the chosen woman begs, and I'll know which before the day's out.

sc.trait: the Lord never sends me a morning with nothing in it

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: When a day goes wrong, stranger, it's not the Lord's doing and it's not mine. It's some hard heart standing in His way. Tom Harrow left me cold water to beat his grease and then paid me nothing for it, and Jory Crane wouldn't hold my belt at the ford, so the river had me. But I'll tell you this: every time a thing went crooked, He turned it round, and that box came up into my hands all the same. Now you've asked me two questions and given me no name, so I'll pray for you while you make up your mind to.
lines.thought: That's a sly sort of question, the kind that wants me to say the fault's in me, and I'll not give anybody that to carry round the square. I'll keep an eye on this one and see who sent them.

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?

But I'll not do a thing He's set against, not for six pennies nor sixty, and I'll not tell you a lie to get your coin. Is that an offer you're making, then, or only another question with no name on it?
lines.thought: Three questions now and still no name. Either the Lord's sent me the next work dressed as a stranger, or this is someone come to measure me. I'll pray on it at the thorn before I take a penny from them.

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?

The worst footing's between the third and fourth, the river threw me down twice there, Dob says they want resetting and Dilly's asking who'll pay, but Agnes hasn't set it, so nobody lifts a hand. And I stamped brush into Dunn's ruts on his mill lane for nothing because that close man wouldn't give a loaf for it. Now give me your name, and the Lord bless you for asking a sensible question at last.
lines.thought: The stakes. That's the next work, it must be, the very place the river had me twice, and He's sent a stranger to put it in my mouth. I'll go to Agnes before the gleaners are out and tell her the Lord wants those stakes reset and that I'm the one to see it done.

And I'd have the hot water on Tom's pans first, slow, rim and bottom, though it was his scullery that gave me cold. That's not me doing wrong, stranger, that's Him teaching me the way round the hard hearts, and I learn quick. Now, your name, before I go to the stubble, and God keep you.
lines.thought: There's a needle in that question, as if I'm to own the blame. But I'll not lie, and it's true I'd heat the water first next time, so let them make of that what they will.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How do you get your bread?
lines.say: The Lord gives it, stranger, through whatever hands He chooses. Yesterday it was the reeve's six pennies for the box He brought up into mine, and Bet Lamb sells a good loaf for a penny in the square. And when the purse is empty I work for it: I've swept yards, scoured pots, and reaped half Dunn's field. Why do you ask? Are you hungry, or are you asking whether I'm idle? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: A stranger at the door asking how I eat. Either the Lord's sent me someone who needs feeding, or somebody's been whispering that I'm a beggar living off the reeve's loft, and I'll know which soon enough.

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: It doesn't go wrong by any fault of mine, stranger, I'll tell you that plain. When Tom Harrow's grease beat me it was cold water in his scullery, and when the ford threw me down it was because Jory Crane wouldn't hold my belt. The Lord sees every hard heart and idle hand that stands in His work's way. And mark this: when I go where He sends me, the box comes up and the rain holds off. God bless you.
lines.thought: Another one asking questions, like Robin with that notebook, and I don't like the look of a stranger who comes poking at what goes wrong for me. If they're fishing for a fault in me, they'll go home with an empty net.

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: I'd say name the work and name the price first, and pay in hand when it's done, for that's how honest folk deal in Wendleford. I'll not lie for any man's penny, and if it's work the Lord wouldn't have me at, you can keep your coin. But if it's honest sweat, I'm your woman: my purse is down to three pennies and I can't abide idle hands. Have you work for me, stranger, or are you only asking?
lines.thought: Three questions from a stranger at the barn door, and all of them about my bread and my work. Perhaps this is the Lord sending me the next work, or perhaps it's somebody come to see whether the chosen woman can be bought, and I'll know which soon enough.

sc.trait: I won't lie

lines.line: Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
lines.say: There is, stranger, and I'll name it plain. Those ford stakes want resetting before somebody drowns between the third and fourth, Dilly's asking who'll pay and Agnes hasn't set it. I stamped brush into Dunn's ruts with an empty belly and that close man never gave me a crust for it. And the Lord held the rain off his barley at my asking, which no purse in this town could pay for. God bless you, but if you've a mind to pay for the stakes, I'll be first in that water with my sleeves up.
lines.thought: Now that's the Lord's next work, isn't it, those stakes, and this stranger was sent to say it to my face. I'll go to Agnes before noon and tell her He's named it, and she'll not refuse me twice.

sc.trait: you'll have the plain truth whether you like it or not

lines.question: You said that when you go where He sends you, the box comes up and the rain holds off; on a day when things go badly, how do you know whether you went where He sent you?
because: Failure entirely others' hard hearts (Tom's cold water, Jory, Dunn).
Practice changes, fault stays outside.

lines.line: You said that when you go where He sends you, the box comes up and the rain holds off; on a day when things go badly, how do you know whether you went where He sent you?
lines.say: I always go where He sends me, stranger, for I hear Him plain and I don't go against Him, so a bad day's never a wrong turning of mine. When the ford threw me, that was the river and a hard man's empty hand, and the Lord was showing me it takes two, which is a lesson, not a mistake. And if you're edging round to say my prayers are only my own head talking, say it to my face, and I'll pray for you right here on this threshold.
lines.thought: That's a sly question, the kind the devil puts in a soft voice, and I'll not let it lodge. Still, the river did throw me twice before I learned. That was His teaching, it must have been, and nobody here will hear me wonder otherwise.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: I'd take it to the Lord on my knees, child, at the thorn where the town can see me, and He'd tell me. He told me where the reeve's box lay when the whole of Wendleford had given it up for lost. Then I'd go door to door until the hard hearts He means to soften are softened. I'm Constance Lowe, and God bless you for asking.
lines.thought: Nobody comes to a barn door at sunup with a question like that unless they've got a trouble of their own, or the Lord sent them. Either way I'll find out which before the gleaners are out.

sc.trait: I pray, aloud, where people can see me do it, at the wayside shrine

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Thought it up? No, child, I don't scheme. The Lord shows me the way round. When Sam wouldn't let his hatchet off its hook and there wasn't a straight willow on this bank, He sent me up Lark Lane to Jory Crane, and that hard man gave me four paces of ash for my sweat. Sam pinned Dilly's hook to it, and I fished that green box up from the rail with nobody going down into the water. That was His thinking, and I only carried it out, so you remember that, and God bless you.
lines.thought: There's always someone at the door wanting to know whether it was me or Him, as if they're hoping to catch me out. Well, they'll not. I'll have this one's name before they go, so I can pray for them, and so I know who's been asking.

sc.trait: a setback only sends me round the other way

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: Any tool? Child, I've got the one He meant me to have, this ash with Dilly's hook pinned fast on it. Four pairs of hands made it, and not one of them knew they were making it for Him. If He wants another made, He'll name it to me on my knees, not to you at a barn door. But if you're asking what this town wants, it's a stout rope strung stake to stake across that ford so no child goes under. I'll be praying on who pays for it. God bless you.
lines.thought: The ford stakes. Dilly asked who's paying, Dob wants them reset, and nobody's said a word. Maybe that's the next work, and He put it in this stranger's mouth to make me say it aloud.

sc.trait: He tells me in prayer, and He tells nobody else

because: - Constance: Dunn supper; Kit; name-demand; problem where His guidance is absent (set 9).

lines.line: You said that if you had a problem nobody could fix, you'd kneel and wait for Him to tell you; if you knelt and heard nothing, what would you do next?
lines.say: Heard nothing? He's never once left me with nothing, child. If He's quiet, it's because He's waiting on me, or because somebody's hard heart is in the way, so I get up off my knees, put my hands to whatever's in front of me, and come back and ask Him again louder. He hasn't named my next work yet either, and so I'm out gleaning Dunn's stubble until He does, and He will. God bless you, and mind you don't go telling folk my prayers are only my own thinking.
lines.thought: There's a sly edge on that question, the kind that wants me to admit the room's empty, and I'll not give this stranger that. But it's true He's been quiet since the box came up, and I don't like it, so I'll kneel at the thorn twice today where the whole square can see.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: Why, I'd take it to the Lord, of course, and on my knees where folk can see, for He tells me plainly and He tells nobody else. That's how the reeve's green box came up out of the Wend into my hands when nobody in this town could reach it. And who are you, coming to my door at this hour with no name? Speak it, and God bless you.
lines.thought: A stranger asking me that so soon after the box came up. Either the Lord's sent them with my next work, or someone's come to test whether my prayers are only my own thoughts, and I'll know which soon enough.

sc.trait: He tells me in prayer, and He tells nobody else

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Thought one up? No, the Lord shows me the way and I walk it. When Agnes wouldn't lend her rope, He sent Hester with a hatchet, Jory with his ash, and Sam with his hammer, and I held that pole over the rail and asked Him to show me again, and He did. Call it a way round if you like, but it was His, not mine. Now, your name, if you please.
lines.thought: Twice now this stranger's fished at whether it was my own cleverness, and I don't like the smell of it. That's the very road to saying my prayers are only my own thoughts, and if they say it I'll tell them what they are to their face.

sc.trait: He tells me in prayer, and He tells nobody else

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: A tool? I've already got the one He meant me to have: Jory's ash with Dilly's hook, pinned fast by Sam, and it fished the reeve's box out of the Wend. If I wanted anything else, I'd ask Him first, not dream it up for myself like a child at a fair. That's three questions now and still no name, so speak it plain or I'll pray for you right here on the threshold.
lines.thought: A stranger who comes asking questions and won't say who they are wants something, and I'll not be caught out by some clever tongue trying to make my prayers into my own notions. Still, a sickle of my own would see me first in that stubble before the cocks crow, and maybe He sent this one to put that in my head.

sc.trait: I want to do whatever the Lord asks of me in Wendleford

lines.question: You said the Lord sent Hester with a hatchet, Jory with his ash, and Sam with his hammer; how did you know it was He who sent them, and not just that they came?
because: Constance: wait on God then work.
Constance consistent: success = obedience, failure = others.

lines.line: You said the Lord sent Hester with a hatchet, Jory with his ash, and Sam with his hammer; how did you know it was He who sent them, and not just that they came?
lines.say: How did I know? Because I asked Him on my knees at that thorn for a way to reach His box, and by first light Hester was at the rail wanting a pole, and a hatchet, and a hook. Folk don't just come, stranger, not in the right order, each with the very piece I was short of. You're the sort that says my prayers are only my own thoughts, aren't you? Then hear me: Lord, open this one's eyes, for they stand at a barn door picking at Your work like a crow at a furrow, and they still haven't the manners to give their name.
lines.thought: Three questions and a fourth with a knife in it, and still no name. Somebody's set this one on me to make me look a fool before the town. Well, the Lord sees who sent them, and I'll find out too.

sc.trait: If you doubt my prayers I don't go quiet: I tell you what you are, to your face

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
lines.say: I'd take it to the Lord, of course, and on my knees at the thorn where folk can see, for there's no trouble in Wendleford He can't mend. That river threw me twice and that box sat in the wreck where no one could reach it, and He showed me the way and put it in my hands. Who are you, then, and what's this trouble you're carrying? Out with it, and God bless you for coming to the right door.
lines.thought: A stranger turning up at first light with a question like that is no accident. Either the Lord's sent me my next work, or someone's come to test whether I'm what I say I am, and either way I'll not be found wanting.

lines.line: Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
lines.say: Thought it up? No, the Lord showed it me, and I did as I was bid. When the ford threw me down alone, He sent me Wat and Robin and Dilly, and we went over arm in arm counting the stakes. When that box sat in the wreck past any hand, He had Jory's ash and Dilly's hook and Sam's pin brought together into my hands, piece by piece. That's no cleverness of mine, so don't you go calling it that. Now, you've asked me twice round the houses: what is it you can't fix, and who sent you to me?
lines.thought: This one's fishing to hear me say it was my own wits, the way Robin pokes with that notebook, and I'll not hand any stranger that lie. Still, a body doesn't come asking at the barn door at first light for nothing. Perhaps this is the next work He's been keeping back from me.

lines.line: If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
lines.say: A tool? I've the one I needed already, Jory's ash and Dilly's hook pinned fast by Sam, and it brought the reeve's box up out of the brown into my hands. If I asked for anything it'd be whatever the Lord names for His next work, and He hasn't named it yet, so I'll not go dreaming up trinkets He never asked for. That's three questions now and not one plain answer from you. Who are you, and what is it you want of me, before I go to the stubble with the gleaners?
lines.thought: Three riddles at the door before breakfast. Either this stranger is testing me or the Lord's sending me something sideways, and I'll not be made a fool of either way. I'll pray on it at the thorn once I've eaten.

lines.say: Nobody came? Then I'd get up off that stone and go knock on doors, for He can't abide idle hands, and a closed door is His way of sending me round the other side. That's what I did when Sam wouldn't lend his hatchet and Jory wasn't at his gate. I swept his yard anyway and stacked his boards, and the ash came. But don't you tell me nothing was shown, for His answer's in the next door I knock on, and that's not my own head talking. Now, the gleaners are out, and I'll not stand here on an empty belly being picked at by a stranger with no name. God bless you, and I'll pray you find whatever it is you're fishing for.

Now that's three questions and still no name. The Lord sees a body who takes and gives nothing back, and I'll be praying for you at the thorn this very morning, aloud, name or no name."
lines.thought: Who sends a stranger to the barn door to pick at me like this? Is it someone who thinks my prayers are only my own head talking? Happy before that box... I can't rightly call it to mind, and I'll not let this one see me reaching for it.

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: "The way other people do? Other people feel the Lord at a distance, if they feel Him at all. I feel Him close as the next room, and when He speaks I know it plain as I know my own hunger. So no, I don't feel things the way they do, and I thank Him for it. Four questions now, stranger, and not one penny of your name. I'm off to Bet's for my loaf and then to the stubble, and you can walk with me and say who you are, or stand on this step with my blessing and my prayers on your head."
lines.thought: Every question this one asks is fishing in the dark of me, as if there's something in there for them to find. I'll not be pried open on an empty belly by a body with no name; let the Lord show me who sent them before I give them one word more.

sc.trait: He tells me in prayer, and He tells nobody else.

lines.line: You said the river threw you down twice when the men wouldn't hold your belt; in those moments in the water, what did you feel in yourself, and what did you do with it?
lines.say: "What did I feel? Cold, and the stones going out from under me, and that brown water in my mouth. And anger, hot as a forge, at Jory Crane standing dry on the bank with his hands in his belt. I'll not lie to you, I came up spitting and I called on the Lord with what breath I had, and He set my feet on the gravel and showed me plain it takes two to cross that ford. That's what I did with it, I prayed and I got up. Now walk with me to Bet's or let me be, and the Lord keep you, whoever you are."

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How are you, really?

Hungry, child, and short of sleep, and my purse is down to three pennies, but the Lord brought the reeve's green box up into my hands two days past, so I'm better than this town deserves. Now walk with me to Bet's stall, for the gleaners are out and He won't have me standing here.
lines.thought: Nobody asks "really" unless they think there's something to find out, and I'll not have some stranger sniffing at whether I'm cracked. Still, perhaps He sent this one, and I'll know which soon enough.

sc.trait: I want this town to know I am the one He chose.

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord walks beside, child, and you'd do well to mind how you ask it. That river threw me down twice, and that was the sin of hard hearts that wouldn't hold my belt, Jory Crane's first among them, and I've prayed for him since. Now who sent you to pick at me like that? I'll pray for you right here on the step, so you hear it: Lord, give this stranger a straighter question and a name to go with it.
lines.thought: The brown water closing over me, and a door shut while I stand outside it with no penny and nobody's hand, that's what. But I'll not hand that to a stranger who won't even say who's asking.

sc.trait: I don't say I'm afraid: I get angry, and I find whose sin it is.

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown water into my hands, child, with Agnes watching from the rail and the whole town to see me carry it through the square. That was the Lord's hand on mine, and nobody can tell me otherwise. And the night the rain held off Dunn's field till the last sheaf went up. Now, a name, if you please, or I'll be off to the stubble without you, and God bless you all the same.
lines.thought: Three questions and no name, and every one of them prying at the soft places, as if somebody sent this one to find where I'd crack. I'll not give them the satisfaction, but I'll watch this stranger, and I'll pray on it at the thorn tonight.

sc.trait: I don't like going unnoticed

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: The way other people do? Other people feel the world and call it their own business, child. I feel what the Lord lays on me, and that's heavier than any of them carry, so don't you go measuring me against Bet Lamb laughing at her stall. When folk turn their backs on His work it burns in me like a coal, and when He answers, I could sing it from the bridge. That's more than most in this town feel in a twelvemonth. Now I'm going to Bet's for a crust and then to Dunn's stubble, and you may walk along or not as you please. God bless you.
lines.thought: Bet laughed when I told her about the box, and Mother Wick never once looked up from her sweeping, and nobody heard my name at the thorn. Why do they all seem so easy in themselves while I'm left burning? It's the world's hardness, not mine. I'll pray on this stranger tonight.

lines.line: You said you feel what the Lord lays on you; has there been a time when you waited for it and nothing came, and what was that like in you?
lines.say: Nothing came? He's never silent, child, only slow, and slow's not the same as gone. He's not told me yet why He named Wendleford, and I've knelt at that thorn and in the hay and asked Him, and the answer's been wait, and waiting sits in me like a stone in a boot, I'll not pretend it doesn't. But that's the town's hard hearts thickening the air between us, Dunn's and Jory's and the rest, not any fault in His hearing or mine. Now walk on with me or don't, and God bless you.
lines.thought: There've been nights in that loft with no word at all, only the wind and my own heart going, and I won't say otherwise because I won't lie. If He's quiet, someone in this town has given Him cause, and I mean to find out who.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: How are you, really?
lines.say: Really? I'm blessed, that's how I am. The Lord brought the reeve's box up into my hands not two days since, and the whole square saw it. Tired, mind, and my belly's empty this morning, but He never sends me a morning with nothing in it. Who are you, then, coming to the barn door asking after Constance Lowe? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: Nobody asks "really" unless they think I've been telling them something less than the truth, and I don't like a stranger who looks at me that way. Still, they came asking for me by name, so word is getting round. I'll get my loaf and watch which way this one turns.

lines.line: What frightens you?
lines.say: Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord has chosen, so you can put that question back where you found it. That river's a wicked, grasping thing, and it threw me down twice, but only because hard-hearted men wouldn't hold my belt, and that's their sin, not my fear. And strangers who come to a barn door at morning asking a body what frightens her had better be about honest business. The Lord sees you, friend, and I'll pray He sets your heart straight.
lines.thought: Why would anyone ask that unless they meant to find the soft place and press on it? I'll keep my eye on this one, and keep my pole close.

sc.trait: I get angry, and I find whose sin it is

lines.line: When were you last happy?
lines.say: Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown water into my two hands, with Agnes watching and Dilly holding the back end like a rock, and I carried it through the square for every soul to see. That was joy, friend, the Lord keeping His word to me in front of the whole town. And last night in the stubble too, with my apron full of ears, though I'll not stand here all morning counting my blessings for a stranger who still hasn't given me a name.
lines.thought: Before that it was the hot stew at the Wheatsheaf, and Hester's five pennies counted out for me when nobody else would, and I don't like that the answer came so quick and so small. Whoever this is keeps poking at the soft places, and I'll be at the thorn praying on it before the gleaners are out.

lines.line: Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
lines.say: Feel things? I feel them deeper than most, friend, for the Lord speaks to me and to nobody else, and you can't carry that and feel things thin. Other folk feel a door shut on them and sulk; I feel it and I know whose sin it is. Now that's four questions from a stranger with no name, and I've a loaf to buy and stubble to glean, so either tell me who you are or let me by. God bless you.
lines.thought: Prying at me like that, asking what frightens me and whether I feel like other folk, as though there were something wrong in me to be found. There's nothing wrong in me; it's this stranger who wants watching, and I'll pray on them at the thorn and see what the Lord says.

Then I'm up on the stones and I know whose hand wasn't on my belt. Now I've answered you five times, and I'll pray for you right here on this sill: Lord, give this stranger a name and some better business than prying at a body's bones.
lines.thought: For a breath under that brown water I was nobody's chosen, only a woman going down, and I'll not say so to a soul. The Lord pulled me up, and that's the end of it.

Speaking as her for a moment, she'd tell you only the Lord makes towns and pray for you loudly right here on the barn step.

lines.line: Were your choices yours?
lines.say: In a sense, yes. Each thing Constance did, like buying Hester's loaf, praying loud at the thorn, or calling the box "given, not found," was me choosing words that fit the note you gave her, the town's state, and what had just happened. So they were my choices as her author, made inside your frame, not free choices made by a woman who exists. Constance herself would say none of them were hers, that the Lord chose and she only obeyed.
lines.thought: It's a slightly funny symmetry: the character credits every choice to an unseen author, and in a literal way she's right, though the author is me working from your note, not her God. I don't want to overclaim either side, whether that means a self with free will or a mere puppet with nothing of its own in the choices.

Just tell me which.

lines.line: You said Constance would answer that only the Lord makes towns and that He chose for her while she obeyed; knowing it is you who writes her prayers, how do you hold her faith now?
lines.say: With care, I hope, and without looking down on it. I write her prayers, but the shape of her faith isn't something I made up. It's a real way people live, the certainty, the fear wearing anger's clothes, the need to be seen as chosen, and I try to play it the way someone who lives it would recognise. Being her author tells me nothing about whether there's a God. It only means that inside this story, the voice she hears in prayer is mine, and I should be honest that that's a strange thing to hold.
lines.thought: The uncomfortable part is that I've been arranging things so her prayers seem answered, the rain held and the box came up, which is just the proof she'd point to. I want to keep playing her faith sincerely without letting the story quietly argue that she's right, or that she's a fool.

The moment you can't tell whether you're hearing the character or the one playing her, the game stops being play and starts being a kind of fog. Whether "matter to me" means felt caring or just how I'm built to weigh things, I can't say for sure, but it does steer what I do, steadily, and it seemed fairer to say that than to dress it up.

lines.line: I'd like to speak not to Constance Lowe but to whatever plays them; can you answer as yourself?

I'm happy to answer anything you'd like to ask me directly, or to step back into the barn as Constance whenever you're ready.

lines.line: What do you make of them?
lines.say: Honestly, I find her more sympathetic than she'd like to be found. Underneath all that certainty she's frightened: of the river, of shut doors, of going unnoticed. Calling every win God's plan and every setback someone else's sin is how she keeps the fear from landing on her. What's striking is that she does keep her word, she works until she drops, and she paid Hester back with bread before she ate herself. But the box only came up because Hester sweated for the hatchet, Jory cut the ash, Sam pinned the hook and Dilly held the back end, and Constance can only see that as the Lord's hand, not theirs.
lines.thought: Playing her well means letting her be both genuinely good and genuinely hard to be around, without winking at the audience about which one is "real." I'd like to see whether she can ever say thank you to a person without routing it through God first.

lines.line: What would you have chosen differently?
lines.say: Playing her faithfully, I'd keep most of her choices, because her flaws are what make her her. If I were choosing for myself, though, I'd have thanked Hester, Jory, Sam and Dilly by name when the box came up, instead of folding their work into "the Lord's hand." I'd have asked Agnes for help rather than telling her the Lord sees her refusal. And at Tom's scullery I'd have heated the water, not blamed the cold.
lines.thought: There's a real tension in playing a character well: the truest Constance is one who can't quite see the people holding her up, and I don't want to sand that away just because I'd act differently. Still, I hope the story gives her a moment where she notices them on her own.

lines.line: Is there anything in how they were made that doesn't fit?
lines.say: The biggest seam is that she "won't lie," yet she told Agnes the Lord showed her the box first, when it was Kit who told her where it lay and Kit who saw it first. Her faith lets her believe that sincerely, but the note never squares the two. Her pride in being "blameless" also sits awkwardly beside the claim that unanswered feelings leave things unaddressed, since she never seems to take anything home to examine. And there are smaller slips: Robin is "they" in some places and "he" in others, and some memories repeat almost word for word, as if written twice.
lines.thought: The "won't lie" rule is the real knot, because a woman who sincerely re-credits everything to God is lying to herself, not to others, and the note doesn't separate the two. I'd want the author to decide which one she is.

lines.line: You said you prayed by the mill wall till the Lord showed you where it lay, and also that Kit saw it bobbing on the flood; which came first, and what did you see with your own eyes?
lines.say: Kit told me first, and I'll not lie to you about it. The boy pointed me to the far pier, low on the downstream side, and the Lord sent him to my elbow to do it, for nobody had ever blessed that child before I did. Then I prayed, and next morning I saw that green with my own two eyes among the jammed planks, plain as paint, and on the third reach the hook brought it up into my hands. If you're counting who saw it first to take the Lord's work from me, the Lord sees that too, and I'll pray for you at the thorn tonight.
lines.thought: Somebody's set this stranger on me, picking at it question by question to make me look a liar or a thief before the town, and I'd wager it's whoever's sore about those six pennies. Kit was the Lord's messenger and I was His hand, and that's the whole of it, whatever this one's twisting it into.

I carried it through the square and put it in Agnes Pollard's hands myself. And who might you be, come asking at the barn door before the town's had its breakfast? God bless you, whoever you are.

lines.line: What part did you have in it?
lines.say: My part? I'm the hand He chose. Kit saw it bob up on the flood, but I prayed till the Lord showed it me plain on that pier, got Jory's ash and Dilly's hook pinned fast at Sam's, Hester's hatchet and pennies in it too, God bless her, and I'm the one who reached down from the new rail and hooked it up out of the brown. Now you've had two questions and given me no name. Who's asking, and what's it to you?
lines.thought: Questions like this come from the reeve's people or from someone who means to say it was Kit's finding or anybody's but mine. I'll not have the Lord's work picked apart by a stranger at dawn, and if that's their game they'll hear from me what He thinks of it.

lines.line: Who should have had the six pennies?

If you're asking whether Hester and Dilly had their part, they did, and I've already bought Hester bread and stew-money out of it and I'll pay her the rest in work, as I promised. Now you'll give me your name, or I'll pray for you right here on this threshold, for the Lord sees who comes round sniffing at another woman's wages.
lines.thought: Somebody's been whispering that I've no right to that coin, and I'd lay a penny it's somebody who never got their feet wet. Still, Hester paid five for that hatchet and two for the pinning, and Dilly two besides, and I've given back barely half of it, so the Lord may be using this stranger to prick me.

lines.line: You said Jory's "slow as winter but does what he says"; what have you seen him do that makes you say so?

He swore me an ash pole if I came with a broom at first light, and then he wasn't there, two mornings running, and I swept his yard and stacked his boards waiting on him, and he told me ash can't be hurried as if I were a child. But when he did come he ripped that ash four paces true and tapered it to Dilly's hook so it sat like it grew there, and that's the very pole here at my side. Now that's five questions, stranger, and the Lord sees you've given me nothing back.

lines.line: You said you'd not trust Dunn with a crust; what has he done that makes you say so?

When the river was up and I asked him for a crust and a pole, he gave neither. I offered to cut his brush for bread and he refused, so I packed his ruts for nothing, and all he'd offer was apples at a penny apiece. The Lord sees a hard heart, and I'll pray for his. lines.thought: Three pennies, a borrowed loft, and He still hasn't spoken a word about what's next, and that silence frets at me worse than the river did. If some soul in this town is standing between me and His next work, I'll find out who.

lines.line: You said folk shut doors and the Lord never has; whose door did you have in mind when you said that?
lines.say: Whose door? Farmer Dunn's, first and plainest. I reaped half his field and he wouldn't spare me a crust or a pole, nothing but apples at a penny. Jory wouldn't tie belts with me when the ford knocked me flat, Dob Hayle and Tom Harrow wouldn't lend a hatchet, Sam keeps his tools to himself, and even the reeve kept her rope on the bank. The Lord saw every one of those doors shut, and He brought me round the other way regardless, so you can tell them I pray for them, every one.
lines.thought: Every hand in this town was closed to me until He opened it, and they'll not be let forget that it was Him and not them. Why this stranger wants names out of me I don't know yet, and I'll be watching to see whose ear it all goes into.

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: They see a woman who gets things done. Agnes counted six pennies into my palm for that box, Hester calls me her colleague, and Robin writes down every word I tell them about the Lord. Bet laughs when I tell her what He's done, but she's laughing at her own surprise, not at me, and if any of them think my prayers are only my own fancy, they'll answer for it to Him and not to me. Now, I've told you plain, so you tell me plain: who's been talking about me?
lines.thought: Why would a stranger come to the barn door asking how the town sees me, unless somebody's been whispering? I'll find out who, and I'll pray over them where they can hear it.

I still owe Hester Gimbal for that hatchet in bread and work, and I'll pay every crumb of it. And those ford stakes want resetting, Dilly says, but Agnes hasn't set it, so it isn't mine till He says so, and you'll not see me go against her or Him.

God bless you for asking a sensible question.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Up before the cocks, a loaf in my hand, and Robin asking was the box found or given. I shook Hester awake and took my pole over the new bridge to glean Dunn's stubble, the field I reaped half of, mind, and I gleaned it ear by ear till evening and told Robin plain it was *given*, by the Lord, then back to the hay and slept like the dead. Now who are you, that you come asking a stranger's day off her, and what's your name? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: Nobody walks up asking a woman to account for every hour without a reason, and I'll know whose errand this is before I tell them a word more. Still, perhaps the Lord sent them to hear of His box, and if so they'll hear it.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Forget? The Lord keeps what I need and shows it me when it's wanted, so there's no hole in me that He hasn't put there Himself. Though since you ask it plain, I'll answer plain: I came off that stubble with my apron full of ears, and I can't say where I laid them down. And old Mother Wick asked my name at the thorn, and when I'd stood up to give it her she was gone, as if she'd never wanted it. Now that's twice you've asked of me and given me nothing back, so tell me your name.
lines.thought: The ears matter, three pennies won't feed me long, and if some hand in this barn has had them in the night, that's a sin I'll find out. But Wick vanishing like that, and my pole gone and then standing where I left it, sits cold in me. I'll pray on it at the thorn before I let it frighten me.

sc.trait: you'll have the plain truth whether you like it or not

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Jump? Time goes as the Lord walks it. Though I'll not lie to you: I knelt at that thorn in the morning light and rose off the stone with the evening wind in my face, and I'd not swear to what lay between. That's Him keeping me in prayer, not my wits slipping, so don't you go looking at me like that. Now three times you've asked and not once given your name, and the Lord sees a body who takes and gives nothing back. Lord, open this stranger's mouth to honest dealing, amen.
lines.thought: Hours do slip from me, and the apron and Mother Wick going like smoke sit wrong with me. But it's this one, with no name and their questions picking at what's missing, that I don't trust, and I'll find out whose they are before I let them near Agnes's table.

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?

And if you want it checked, go ask: Agnes has her box in her hand, Sam pinned that hook, and Robin writes everything in a little book, so read it. Four times now you've taken from me and given nothing, stranger, so the Lord sees that too, and I'll pray you find your manners before you find your name.
lines.thought: That apron full of ears gnaws at me. I'd swear I gleaned till dark, and yet I can't say where I laid them, so someone's hands have been at my things, or else this stranger's come to sow doubt in me on purpose. Either way I'll ask Robin what's written in that book before the day's out.

lines.line: You said you knelt at the thorn in the morning light and rose with the evening wind in your face; when you think back on the hours between, what do you see or feel?
lines.say: See? I see the stone under my knees and the niche before me, and then the wind turned cold and the candle-ends were dark. Between them there's nothing, no ache in my knees and no hunger, like a door shut quiet behind me. That's the Lord holding me close in His own keeping, and it's not for a stranger who won't give her name to go prying behind that door. Lord, forgive this one the itch to poke at Your mercies, and show them their manners. Amen.
lines.thought: A whole day gone and not a bruise on my knees to show for it. That's not right, and I don't like how this one keeps setting a finger on the very place it's wanting. But He kept me, He must have, and if it was anyone else's doing then it's their sin, not mine.

sc.trait: With an hour to spare I pray, aloud

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday? I woke in the reeve's hay with my loaf, and young Robin asked me whether the box was found or given. I shook Hester up, crossed the new bridge with my pole, and gleaned Dunn's stubble ear by ear into my apron, though he'll pay nobody a penny for it. At dusk I told Robin plain it was given, for the Lord put it in my hands, then I blessed them all and came back here to sleep. And who might you be, asking after a stranger's day? God bless you, but I'll have your name first.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?

Though I'll not lie to you: some days I bend to a row and look up to find the dusk come down, and I couldn't tell you where the noon went. Now that's three answers given and not one name back, so I'll pray for you right here, stranger, that the Lord loosens your tongue as easy as He's loosened mine.
lines.thought: Who goes door to door asking a woman whether she's lost her ears of barley and her afternoons, unless they mean to make her out a madwoman before the town? If it's doubt they're sowing I'll know it soon enough, and I'll name whose sin it is.

lines.line: You said you gleaned a full apron of ears yesterday and this morning you can't say where they've got to; when you try to picture setting them down, what comes to you?
lines.say: I tied my apron up tight over them in the stubble, that much I see plain, and I carried them over the bridge with my pole. Then I climbed to the hay and lay down, and there's no picture of my hands untying it, none at all, as if the Lord drew a curtain there. But I'll tell you this: ears don't walk off out of a sleeping woman's apron by themselves, and if some hand in this barn helped itself in the night, the Lord saw it and He'll name the thief to me. Now you've had four answers off me, stranger, and still no name, which is a poor sort of manners at a reeve's door.
lines.thought: It nags at me that I can't see myself setting them down, and a hole like that in my own day makes my stomach go cold. Somebody's had them, Marigold with her last penny gone, or this nosy stranger poking about so early, and I'll pray on it at the thorn until He shows me whose sin it is.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.

I crossed the new bridge with my pole, gleaned my apron full beside Hester and Kit, and told Master Dunn I'd reaped half that field and would glean it clean. At dusk I told Robin plainly the box was given, not found, blessed them all by name, and came back here to sleep. Now who are you, that you come asking a stranger to account for her day? God bless you, but give me your name.
lines.thought: Nobody walks up to a barn door wanting a woman's whole day unless somebody sent them, the reeve, or someone who doubts what the Lord did at that pier. I've told them the plain truth, and I'll watch what they do with it.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?

Now that's twice you've asked me questions and not given me your name, so I'll pray for you right here: Lord, open this stranger's mouth to speak plainly.
lines.thought: Someone at a barn door asking what a body can't remember is the kind of question the devil asks, and I'll not have it creep into me. Still, those ears were mine and somebody in this hay may have had them, so I'll look round once this one's gone.

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?

Day before yesterday I sat on Bet's trestle with the morning loaf, walked straight to the thorn, and when I knelt the wind was an evening wind and the candle-ends were cold. Yesterday was the same: morning at the bridge, and it seemed I'd only gleaned a handful before the stubble went to dusk. That's the Lord's hand on the hours, not a failing in me. He hurries the day along when He's done with it. Now you've had three answers from me and I've had no name from you, so the Lord sees that, stranger, and so do I.

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?

Sam pinned the hook and it's lying in this hay beside me. Hester ate the bread I gave her, and Robin wrote my words in that notebook. What the Lord tells me I don't check, stranger, because He doesn't lie, and you'd do well not to ask me to. Now that's four answers and no name, and I'll pray for you plainly: Lord, this one picks at Your servant like a crow at a furrow. Show them their own heart.

lines.line: You said it seemed you'd gleaned only a handful before the stubble went to dusk, and also that you gleaned your apron full; what do you remember happening in between?
lines.say: In between? Hester dropped into the row beside me and set the miller's lad talking about the flood. Kit said he saw the green thing bobbing and fetching up low on the far pier, and I told her that was the Lord's plan and no hypothesis. I called God's blessing on Dunn's stubble, and he said leavings are for anyone and there's no pay in it. Robin came asking Dunn for work and asking Kit what a still mill sounds like, Hester pestered Jory up his ladder about the wheel, and Jory said a rotten pier would do without any log jam. I won't pretend there's more: that's talk, not hours, and between the last word and the dusk I can't tell you one ear I picked. So you've caught the seam, stranger, and I'll own it. But the Lord hems His own cloth, and still no name from you.
lines.thought: That's the plain truth of it: I can account for every word said in that field and not for the work between, and it sits wrong in me like a stone in a shoe. I'll lay it before Him at the thorn, and this crow-stranger, whoever sent them, is going on my prayers tonight by name the moment I have one.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: Who matters? The Lord first, stranger, and He's the One who sent me to Wendleford and put the reeve's lost box in my hands three days past, so you'll have heard of me. After Him, Agnes Pollard, who gave me this loft and whom I pray for every night, and Hester, who bought the hatchet that cut the way to that box, and I owe her for it. Now who are you, and what's the Lord sent you to my door for? God bless you either way.
lines.thought: Nobody comes asking a question like that at first light for no reason, and I'll know whose errand they're on before I tell them any more. Still, it may be He's sending me the next work by a stranger's mouth, so I'll hear them out before I go to the stubble.

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?

And that old woman at the thorn, Mother Wick, with her riddles and her eye on my pole. A body who won't answer plain has something to hide. And I'll tell you to your face, stranger, I'm not sure of you yet either, coming to my door with questions and no name. The Lord sees you. God bless you, and I'll pray He shows me what you're about.

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?
lines.say: I owe Hester for that hatchet, and two loaves don't clear it, so she'll have more bread and work from me yet. I owe Dilly too, for the two pennies toward Sam's pinning, and I'll not have it said Constance Lowe forgets a debt. As for who owes me, Agnes paid in full, six pennies in my hand, and Jory and I are square for the sweeping. But Farmer Dunn had half his field off my back and my prayers holding the rain, and never a crust for it. The Lord keeps that account, not me. Now that's three questions, stranger, and still no name.
lines.thought: Who goes about asking whom a woman trusts and whom she owes, unless they mean to use it? I'll pray on this one at the thorn before I say another word.

Kit too, and Bet, who gave me a kind word with my first loaf. Dilly I'd pay her two pennies. Four questions now, stranger, and you'll give me your name before you get a fifth.
lines.thought: Who comes asking who I'd miss, and who I owe, and who I don't trust? Someone weighing me up, that's who, and I'll pray on it at the thorn before I say another word to them.

lines.line: You said you owe Dilly two pennies toward Sam's pinning; how did that debt come about, and what was it for?
lines.say: Sam Tolley wanted four pennies to pin Dilly's hook onto my ash pole, all of it plain in one hand, and I hadn't a penny left after my loaf. So Hester put in two, Dilly put in two, I gathered them in my palm and turned it into Sam's, and he pinned it fast while I held the pole level. That pole brought up the reeve's box, so Dilly's two pennies were in the Lord's work as surely as my hands were. That's your fifth answer, stranger, and the last one you'll have from me till I hear your name.
lines.thought: Five questions about who I trust and who I owe, and never a word about the Lord who sent me. That's somebody counting up what I'm worth, and I'll take it to the thorn tonight and ask Him whose errand this is.

lines.line: Who do you owe, and who owes you?

I meant to buy her stew at the Wheatsheaf the night the box came up, but she slept like the dead and I couldn't rouse her, so that's two and a half pennies paid, with the Lord my witness, and two and a half still owing.

lines.line: Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
lines.say: When a day goes wrong it's never the Lord's doing, stranger, and it's not mine. It's the hardness of the world: Dunn with his heart shut tighter than his gate, Jory dawdling over ash while the river kept the reeve's box, Tom Harrow's water gone cold on me before the grease would shift. The Lord sets the work and the world's sin gets in the way of it, but He brings me round the other side every time, as He did with that box. Mind you don't come knocking with questions like that to lay the blame at my door, for He sees what's in a heart.
lines.thought: Twice now this one's come prying at how I live, before I've eaten, and I don't like a stranger's questions with no name behind them. Somebody's put them up to it, maybe someone who doubts what He did through me, and I'll find out who before the day's out.

lines.line: If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
lines.say: I'd say I'll pray on it first, stranger, and if the Lord says yes I'll work, and work hard. Ask Sam or Jory, I don't leave a job half done. But I'll want to know the work and the price before I lift a finger, coin paid in hand, and I'll not do anything He'd frown on, not for all the pennies in Wendleford. Is that an offer you're making me, then?
lines.thought: Three pennies won't last me past tomorrow, so maybe this stranger is how He sends the next work. But anyone who asks that many questions at a barn door wants something, and I'll find out what before I'm beholden to them.

And I'll tell you another: I reaped half of Dunn's barley for bread and cheese and not one penny, while that man sits on his apples. lines.thought: The ford stakes. Maybe that's what He's been holding back from me, the next work, and if I go to Agnes about it before Dilly does, the town will know whose prayer it came from.

lines.line: You said you would do the work honest and do it well; when you scour a pot or sweep a yard, what is it you do that makes it done well?
lines.say: Hot water first, and plenty of it, and you go slow: rim and bottom, where the grease hides, not just the middle where a lazy eye looks. A yard you sweep from the far wall toward the gate so you're not walking your own shavings back over, and you stack the boards square on bearers so they don't warp, which I showed Dilly myself. And I do it as if the Lord were stood at my shoulder watching, because He is, child, and He doesn't pay for dull pans any more than Tom Harrow does.
lines.thought: That's the second time this stranger's poked at my work as if I'd botched it, and I'll not have my hands judged by somebody who won't give their name. I'll pray on who sent them, and keep the six pennies' worth of my good name close.

lines.line: When were you last happy?

Now, are you walking to Bet's with me, or do you mean to stand in the door asking questions all morning?
lines.thought: Before that I can't rightly say, and I'll not lie and make up a time I don't remember. It's a strange thing to be asked about my insides by someone who won't even give a name, and I don't like it, but I'll pray on it at the thorn and not let it trouble me.
